doc.title: Sol Yaged interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: State of jazz today, WNEW, Coltrane and Miles Davis
summary: Sol dislikes today's radio, and talks about emotion in Coltrane and Miles Davis.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What do you feel about the state of jazz music today? Do you listen to any of the local radio stations and do you like what you hear?

I particularly don’t like what I hear anymore, Monk. I listened to a radio station all my life, for 50 years, WNEW, with a man called Martin Block. And he played the greatest of them all. He played Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, Jan Savitt. He played the greatest bands of all. Glen Gray and the Casa Loma Band. You don’t hear those records anymore. You don’t hear that kind of music anymore.
Well jazz in some sense became, in the 60’s it became kind of political. It became sometimes angry. Do you think —
Well when I think of fellas like Coltrane and that, it’s like they were — it was very, very emotional.

And a style like Miles Davis, you’re right, very emotional. I didn’t know John Coltrane. I knew Miles Davis when I was playing. When I was playing at Jimmy Ryan’s he was across the street at a place called The Three Deuces. Miles Davis. But believe me in those days, and it was only the late 40s, they were angry and hostile too.
I think it was 1946, quite a significant number of the big bands bit the dust.
In the late 40s. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
